questions.prompt: In Frank Jackson's "Mary's room" thought experiment, what does Mary know before she leaves her black-and-white room?

options.text: All the physical facts about color and color vision, although she has never seen color
Nothing about color science
options.why_wrong: The setup requires that she knows all the physical facts.

options.text: Only what other people say about their color experiences
options.why_wrong: She has complete physical knowledge, not just testimony.

options.text: How to see colors by imagining them
options.why_wrong: She has never had color experiences to draw on.

questions.explanation: Mary is a brilliant scientist who knows every physical fact about color vision but has only ever seen black and white. The question is whether she learns something new when she first sees red.

sources.citation: Jackson, F. (1982). Epiphenomenal qualia. The Philosophical Quarterly, 32(127), 127-136.
Nida-Rümelin, M., & O Conaill, D. Qualia: The knowledge argument. In E. N. Zalta (Ed.), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

questions.prompt: What conclusion did Jackson originally draw from the Mary case?
questions.answer_text: That physicalism is false: when Mary first sees color she learns a fact about experience that is not a physical fact.
questions.explanation: Jackson argued that complete physical knowledge leaves out something, the qualia of experience. He later rejected the argument and came to defend physicalism.

sources.citation: Jackson, F. (1982). Epiphenomenal qualia. The Philosophical Quarterly, 32(127), 127-136.
Jackson, F. (1998). Postscript on qualia. In Mind, Method and Conditionals: Selected Essays. Routledge.

questions.prompt: In Frank Jackson's thought experiment, what is the name of the color scientist who has never seen color?
questions.explanation: Jackson's Mary knows every physical fact about color vision but has lived in a black-and-white room; the question is whether she learns something new on first seeing red.

sources.citation: Jackson, F. (1982). Epiphenomenal qualia. The Philosophical Quarterly, 32(127), 127-136.
Nida-Rümelin, M., & O Conaill, D. Qualia: The knowledge argument. In E. N. Zalta (Ed.), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of Jackson's knowledge argument in order.
items: Mary knows all the physical facts about color vision
Mary leaves the room and sees red for the first time
She learns something new: what it is like to see red
So not all facts are physical facts
questions.explanation: Jackson's original argument moves from complete physical knowledge, through Mary's new experience, to the conclusion that some facts are not physical. He later rejected the argument.

sources.citation: Jackson, F. (1982). Epiphenomenal qualia. The Philosophical Quarterly, 32(127), 127-136.
Nida-Rümelin, M., & O Conaill, D. Qualia: The knowledge argument. In E. N. Zalta (Ed.), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

questions.prompt: What does Jackson (1982) conclude from the case of Mary, the colour scientist raised in a black-and-white room?

options.text: Colour vision depends on early visual experience
options.why_wrong: The argument is about knowledge and facts, not developmental neuroscience.

options.text: Mary learns nothing new on seeing red, so physicalism is safe
options.why_wrong: That is the Type-A reply to the argument.

options.text: Not all facts are physical facts, so physicalism is false
Mary gains only a new ability, not new knowledge
options.why_wrong: That is the ability hypothesis, a reply to the argument.

questions.explanation: Mary knows every physical fact about colour vision, yet on seeing red she seems to learn something new: what red is like. If complete physical knowledge leaves a fact out, the argument concludes, there are non-physical facts.

sources.citation: Jackson, F. (1982). Epiphenomenal qualia. The Philosophical Quarterly 32(127), 127-136.
Jackson, F. (1986). What Mary didn't know. The Journal of Philosophy 83(5), 291-295.

questions.prompt: According to the ability hypothesis (Lewis; Nemirow), what does Mary gain on leaving her room?

options.text: New abilities to recognise, imagine and remember red, not a new fact
A new fact about red, which shows physicalism is false
options.why_wrong: That is Jackson's original conclusion, which the hypothesis rejects.

options.text: An old physical fact grasped under a new phenomenal concept
options.why_wrong: That is the phenomenal concepts reply, a different strategy.

options.text: Nothing at all, since she already knew what red is like
options.why_wrong: The ability hypothesis grants that she gains something, only not factual knowledge.

questions.explanation: Knowing what red is like is treated as know-how rather than knowing-that, like riding a bicycle versus knowing it has two wheels. Since Mary gains no new information, physicalism is untouched.

sources.citation: Lewis, D. (1988). What experience teaches. Proceedings of the Russellian Society 13, 29-57.
Nemirow, L. (1990). Physicalism and the cognitive role of acquaintance. In W. G. Lycan (ed.), Mind and Cognition. Oxford: Blackwell.

questions.prompt: On the phenomenal concepts strategy, what does Mary learn when she first sees red?

options.text: A new non-physical fact about red
Only a new ability, not anything factual
options.why_wrong: That is the ability hypothesis, which denies she acquires knowledge-that.

options.text: Nothing, because the scenario is incoherent
options.why_wrong: The strategy accepts the scenario and reinterprets what she learns.

options.text: An old physical fact under a new, first-person concept

questions.explanation: She acquires a phenomenal concept that picks out a brain state she already knew about under a physical description, as 'water' and 'H₂O' pick out one substance. So something real is learned, but no new fact.

sources.citation: Loar, B. (1990). Phenomenal states. Philosophical Perspectives 4, 81-108.
Papineau, D. (2002). Thinking about Consciousness. Oxford University Press.

questions.prompt: What happened to Frank Jackson's own view of the knowledge argument?
questions.answer_text: He later abandoned it and became a physicalist.
questions.explanation: Jackson came to think that the intuition that Mary learns a new fact must be mistaken, and argued for a representationalist physicalism. The argument is still widely discussed independently of its author's later view.

sources.citation: Jackson, F. (1998). Postscript on qualia. In Mind, Method and Conditionals: Selected Essays. London: Routledge.

questions.prompt: In what year did Frank Jackson publish "Epiphenomenal Qualia", which introduced Mary the colour scientist?
questions.explanation: Jackson presented the knowledge argument in "Epiphenomenal Qualia" in 1982, eight years after Nagel's bat paper.

sources.citation: Jackson, F. (1982). Epiphenomenal qualia. Philosophical Quarterly, 32(127), 127-136.

questions.prompt: Mary has learned every physical fact about colour vision inside this black-and-white room. According to Jackson, what happens when she steps out and sees the red tomato?

media.alt: A room in shades of grey with a person reading at a desk and a grey monitor; through an open door a single red tomato is visible

options.text: She learns something new: what it is like to see red
Nothing: she already knew everything about seeing red
options.why_wrong: That is the physicalist reply Jackson argues against in 1982.

options.text: She cannot see colour, because her eyes never developed it
options.why_wrong: The thought experiment assumes normal colour vision.

options.text: She forgets the physical facts she learned
options.why_wrong: The argument turns on gaining knowledge, not losing it.

questions.explanation: Jackson argued that Mary learns a new fact on seeing red, so the physical facts are not all the facts; critics reply that she gains a new ability or a new way of knowing an old fact.

sources.citation: Jackson, F. (1982). Epiphenomenal qualia. Philosophical Quarterly, 32(127), 127-136.
